stories.headline: Carlos Sainz on F1 season concluding in Middle East: 'Very difficult to be convinced right now'
stories.summary: Carlos Sainz said "it's very difficult to be convinced" Formula 1 should finish the season in the Middle East as is currently planned.
stories.body:
Carlos Sainz said "it's very difficult to be convinced" Formula 1 should finish the season in the Middle East as is currently planned.

F1 is currently scheduled to with race in Qatar on Nov. 29 and Abu Dhabi on Dec. 6. despite ongoing hostilities and tensions in the region.

F1 has held off making a call on whether to go ahead but has a plan to race in Imola on Dec. 6 if it needs to cancel the Middle East leg of events.

Sources have told ESPN teams are preparing to race as normal but there is lingering confusion about the lack of clarity.

On Thursday, Grand Prix Drivers Association (GPDA) chairman Sainz appeared to suggest he felt uneasy about going as things stand.

"On my personal side, I'm not speaking as a GPDA [representative], it's very difficult to be convinced right now, because there are still things happening, plenty of things happening in the Middle East," he said.

"And also there is obviously an election that is going to happen in the U.S. [midterms on Nov. 3], and things that are going to happen in the political side of the world that could affect the next month, month and a half, very suddenly.

"So I think it's relatively premature to be so convinced, but as it stands, we will go to Qatar and Abu Dhabi, and if the FIA and Formula 1 decide that it's still safe and a good scenario, I think we, as drivers, have to go with whatever they say.

"We don't have as much political information, as much inside information as they have, for sure, so we need to follow their lead and trust in their decision-making, but only as it stands.

- Kimi Antonelli is on the brink of F1 history -- but first, there's a car to wash and pranks to pull

- British teenager Freddie Slater to make F1 practice debut for Audi in Mexico and Brazil

- Christian Horner to Mercedes? Ex-Red Bull boss reveals pre-Toto Wolff approach

"The world can change a lot in the next month, month and a half, and we need to stay diligent and reactive to whatever happens, and not just go because we want to go right now."

A few hours later, Williams posted a quote from Sainz where he clarified the comments and reiterated his full faith in the sport's decision-makers.

"Following some reporting of my comments in the press conference earlier today about ending the season in the Middle East, I want to be clear that I know the FIA and Formula 1 will put safety first and completely trust them to make the right decision. We look forward to racing in Qatar and Abu Dhabi."

stories.headline: Shai Gilgeous-Alexander's record 20-point streak ends in Thunder win over Nuggets
stories.summary: Shai Gilgeous-Alexander's historic streak of 20-point games ended Thursday night when he finished with 17 in a 96-84 win over the Nuggets.
stories.body:
Oklahoma City Thunder star Shai Gilgeous-Alexander had his first game with fewer than 20 points in nearly two years, finishing with 17 in Thursday night's 96-84 home win over the Denver Nuggets to snap his NBA-record streak of 20-point games.

Gilgeous-Alexander, who scored 32 points in a convincing win over San Antonio on Tuesday night, shot just 6 of 19 from the field against Denver in failing to reach 20 points for the first time since Oct. 30, 2024, a streak of 141 regular-season games.

He had just under two minutes left to score three more points and extend his streak, but with Oklahoma City up 93-76 with 1:43 left, he asked Thunder coach Mark Daigneault to sub him out.

"I was going to go out there, and then I saw that [the Nuggets] had subbed, so I thought we should sub, too," Gilgeous-Alexander said. "You always treat the game with respect."

Daigneault said he wanted to leave Gilgeous-Alexander in the game because a "historic streak" was on the line and praised his star player's maturity.

"I just think of the class that it shows and the perspective that it shows for him to say, 'Hey, I'm out now. The game's calling for me to be subbed out,'" Daigneault said. "That was his substitution. And of all the things that I admire about him, that's toward the top of the list in terms of moments that I appreciate about him."

Gilgeous-Alexander, the league's two-time reigning MVP, missed all seven shots he took in the first 24 minutes Thursday night as the Thunder trailed by as many as nine points. A pair of free throws kept him from going scoreless in a half for the first time since his rookie season with the LA Clippers in 2019.

It marked just the fourth time in 450 games with the Thunder that he has gone without a field goal in a half. Gilgeous-Alexander scored the first basket of the third quarter to pull Oklahoma City to 48-46.

Aaron Gordon scored 20 points, and Nikola Jokic and DeMar DeRozan added 13 apiece for Denver, which was playing its first game.

A layup by Ajay Mitchell gave the Thunder a 64-62 lead -- their first since 3-0 -- and 3-pointers by Alex Caruso and Gilgeous-Alexander extended it to 70-64 after three quarters. Oklahoma City pushed the advantage to 93-76 on a 3 by Gilgeous-Alexander to give him 17 points with 1:44 left. He then asked to be taken out during a timeout and did not return to the game.

Jalen Williams scored 21 points, and Chet Holmgren had 12 points and 17 rebounds for the Thunder.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

stories.headline: Caleb Williams throws 2 TD passes as the Bears beat Drake Maye and the Patriots 30-24
stories.summary: — Round 2 went to Caleb Williams and the Chicago Bears.
stories.body:
CHICAGO -- — Round 2 went to Caleb Williams and the Chicago Bears.


Williams passed for 308 yards and two touchdowns, and the Bears cooled off Drake Maye and the New England Patriots with a 30-24 victory Thursday night.


It was the second meeting between the young quarterbacks since they were part of the 2024 NFL draft. Maye, who was selected by New England at No. 3, directed the Patriots to a 19-3 victory over Williams and the Bears when the longtime friends were rookies.


But Williams, the No. 1 overall pick, leaned on Luther Burden and Colston Loveland while outlasting Maye and the Patriots in the rematch. Williams connected on 22 of 33 passes in his second game back after being sidelined by a right hamstring injury.


“These nights are awesome,” Williams said. “You play against another good team on a primetime game in a short week, these games are awesome because you get to see who you are as a team. That’s who we are. We’re a smashmouth football team, an innovative team. And when things happen and things don’t go our way and the water is rocky, we stay steady.”


Maye was 24 for 31 for 321 yards and two touchdowns. He also had a 7-yard run for New England's first TD with 11:33 left in the first half.


But Maye also was intercepted by Bears linebacker D'Marco Jackson in the end zone on a pass intended for rookie tight end Eli Raridon late in the second quarter.


“It’s those plays, I talk about it all the time,” Maye said. “You know those plays that can swing the game, can impact the game and that was definitely one of them right there. Yeah, I wish I definitely had that one back.”


New England (4-3) had won three consecutive games behind Maye, who threw 10 TD passes and one interception during the win streak.


“He gave us a chance," Patriots coach Mike Vrabel said. "He competed and I know he’d like to have that throw back to Eli, but I thought he really competed. Whether that was running around and scrambling or finding good places to go with the football. He gave us a chance. ... I’m glad he’s ours.”


Burden had four catches for 130 yards for Chicago (5-2), and Loveland had a 12-yard touchdown reception. Cairo Santos kicked a 58-yard field goal with 1:34 left, a career long and matching the franchise record, after he missed a 53-yard attempt earlier in the final quarter.


Williams became the first Bears quarterback to throw for more than 300 yards in consecutive games since Mitch Trubisky had a three-game run in 2018.


“I think he did a pretty good job throughout the night,” Bears coach Ben Johnson said. “I know he had a number of explosive plays. He found some of those guys at the second level that were huge for us.”


After Santos’ long field goal, Maye drove New England into range for Andy Borregales’ 47-yarder with 37 seconds to go. But Chicago recovered the ensuing onside kick.


Rhamondre Stevenson had five catches for 93 yards and a touchdown for the Patriots. Raridon had a 30-yard TD catch in the third quarter.


“We did some good things,” Vrabel said. “But again, didn’t do enough.”


It was Chicago’s first home game since Mike Ditka died on Oct. 9. The Bears saluted the Hall of Fame tight end and longtime coach with a pregame moment of silence, and they also handed out fake mustaches to the crowd of 60,520 at Soldier Field.


Ditka’s No. 89 jersey dotted the stands, and fans also donned Bears sweaters in a callback to what he wore on the sideline as a coach.


Chicago opened a 20-7 lead on Burden’s 24-yard touchdown with 14 seconds left in the first half. Burden got the ball on a screen on third-and-17, and Loveland, Kalif Raymond and Darnell Wright helped clear the way for his second TD reception of the season.


“The whole calvary came ... and it was like a wave carrying him through there,” Johnson said. “He saw a little crease and hit the jets.”


Set to receive the second-half kickoff, the Bears were in position to pull away. But the Patriots responded with Stevenson’s 48-yard touchdown reception on the final play of the period.


Stevenson slipped out of the backfield and Maye lobbed the ball over the head of Bears safety Cam Lewis. Stevenson ran away from Lewis and got a downfield block from DeMario Douglas before cutting past Bears cornerback Jaylon Johnson on his way to the end zone.


Injuries
Patriots: CB Christian Gonzalez played after being listed as questionable because of an illness. ... S Kevin Byard departed after he was checked out by trainers with 9:44 left in first half. He later returned. ... DT Christian Barmore departed late in the game.


Bears: CB Malik Muhammad left in the third quarter with a toe injury. ... TE Cole Kmet hurt his right knee on a reception with 5:34 left. "We’ll know more tomorrow, but I don’t think it looked very good,” Johnson said.


Up next
Patriots: At Miami on Nov. 1.


Bears: At Seattle for a Monday night game Nov. 2.

stories.headline: Mackie Samoskevich's late goal lifts Kraken over Mammoth 5-3
stories.summary: — Mackie Samoskevich scored with 5:25 left, and the Seattle Kraken, despite blowing a multiple-goal third-period lead for the second game in a row, beat the Utah Mammoth 5-3 on Thursday night.
stories.body:
SEATTLE -- — Mackie Samoskevich scored with 5:25 left, and the Seattle Kraken, despite blowing a multiple-goal third-period lead for the second game in a row, beat the Utah Mammoth 5-3 on Thursday night.


The Kraken (7-3-1) carried a 3-1 lead into the third against Utah (7-4-0). On Tuesday. Seattle was up 3-0 heading into the final 20 minutes against Detroit before winning in a shootout, 4-3.


Jordan Eberle and Brandon Montour each had a goal and an assist. Matty Beniers and Frederick Gaudreau also scored, Gaudreau’s going into an empty net with 1:00 left in the game for his team-leading sixth of the season.


Logan Cooley had two goals for the Mammoth, and Vincent Trocheck scored once.


Philipp Grubauer made 33 saves for Seattle.


With the scored tied at 3-3 after each team had a goal taken down in the third on successful offside challenges, Bobby McMann stole the puck near center ice and skated down the left side His shot was deflected wide but the rebound bounced in front of the net. McMann finally got a stick to it, tapping it over to Samoskevich, who pushed it in for his fifth of the year.


Eberle’s fourth goal of the year put Seattle on top just 3:38 into the game. His hard shot from the blue line bounced off the boards, ricocheted off the back of Mammoth goalie Karel Vejmelka, dribbled down his back and into the net. Trocheck tied it for Utah with 2:03 left in the first period.


That tie lasted just 26 seconds before Beniers put the Kraken back in front with 1:37 to go, his third of the season. Montour, who was goalless before scoring on Tuesday against Detroit, made it 3-1 on a power play at 2:23 of the second.


Cooley’s goals, his second and third of the season, came just 27 seconds into the third period and at 7:42 to tie it at 3-3.


Vejmelka made 18 saves.


Up next
Kraken: Host Minnesota on Saturday.


Mammoth: Host Tampa Bay on Saturday.

stories.headline: Consensus top AFL draft prospect Dougie Cochrane already in rare air
stories.summary: Missing significant chunks of football hasn't stopped Port Adelaide NGA star Dougie Cochrane from firming as the top prospect in this year's AFL Draft.
stories.body:
It's rare for a player to be the consensus no. 1 rated prospect in their draft. From coaches to recruiters and a myriad of draft evaluators, Dougie Cochrane stands atop 2026's crop. For him to do so after playing just four games in his top-age campaign puts the Port Adelaide NGA gun in rare air.

The starring junior missed both years of his u18 national championships through injury, and this year only returned to the field in the final month of the season. But what he produced at league level last season and amongst his peers at the u16s national championships in 2024 is not easily forgotten.

Clearly a class above at the national championships three years ago, Cochrane put all of his skill and athleticism on show. He was a distributor out of defence, won aerial duels around the ground and was the focal point of the SA forward line in a showing of his unique versatility.

From there he made his league debut for Central Districts as a 17-year-old, kicking four goals including an outrageous snap on his left foot from the pocket after crumbing a forward 50 contest. From his first game he was already the best player on the ground.

Speaking to ESPN ahead of the draft combine Cochrane was a bit flat. It wasn't because he'd missed his top-age season, he knew he wasn't going to be testing, and he knew most clubs wouldn't bother booking an interview given his ties to Port Adelaide. But there was one thing that really got to him.

"They measured me at 194-and-a-half centimetres," he tells ESPN with a grin. "They took a centimetre off me, but we'll round that up."

At six-foot-four (we'll round it up too) he's widely considered the next elite key forward prospect to come through the AFL Draft. Only he doesn't necessarily see it that way.

"I want to be a midfielder when I'm older, that's what I'm striving towards. "For right now I'm pretty happy forward, if not back. I'm happy wherever the team needs, whatever the team needs.

"I'm pretty skinny right now, I'm not as muscly as the Patty Cripps's of the world, the Bonts of the world. I want to focus on my midfield craft and get that experience."

Cochrane missed a significant chunk of his bottom-age year with a hamstring and over the off-season underwent knee surgery to address patella tendinitis. He didn't play for 11 straight months from the end of 2025 to July 2026.

Watching from the sidelines frustrated him but he knew it was all out of an abundance of caution.

"I started playing league at Centrals last year, I sort of started feeling [knee pain] a little bit. I thought nothing of it, just thought it was a bit of growing pain. It got worse and worse by the time I started doing pre-season... when you take off and do your powerful stuff it flares up.

"They did a clean out of it... I had the surgery, and I walked out of the surgery. It was two little key holes."

Cochrane sat down with ESPN as Port Adelaide list manager Jason Cripps all but confirmed on Trade Radio Essendon would be bidding on the gun academy prospect at pick one in the 2026 AFL Draft.

He's the son of Port Adelaide and North Melbourne midfielder Stuart Cochrane, and grew up supporting the Power after his dad's playing career finished up. His brother Tom was on the list during formative years and the club is set up to match his bid wherever it lands.

"Dad's been my idol growing up. Looking up to him, I obviously didn't get to see him play but he's been enormous."

Asked if it would mean more being that first selection on November 19, Cochrane's humble nature shines through.

"I loved watching the draft growing up, seeing those high picks. The pick doesn't really matter, does it? There have been a lot of picks over times where the number one picks haven't gone as well as they should've. I just want to end up at an AFL club - wherever that is I don't mind - but I just want to play footy," he says.

"Growing up and supporting Port all my life, it would be special playing for them. But whatever happens happens and I'm just gonna let that decide itself."

stories.headline: Stephen Vogt back to Guardians in '27, shuns Mariners rumors
stories.summary: Guardians manager Stephen Vogt dispelled speculation about his future, saying he'll return next season to chase an elusive World Series title.
stories.body:
CLEVELAND -- Guardians manager Stephen Vogt dispelled speculation about his future, saying he'll return to the club next season to chase an elusive World Series title.

"I'm here," Vogt said at a news conference Thursday. "I'm coming back."

Vogt has led the Guardians to a division crown in each of his three seasons, He has twice been named American League Manager of the Year. With the Seattle Mariners' managerial spot open, there had been rumblings about Vogt possibly leaving in order to be closer to his family's home in Olympia, Washington.

However, the 41-year-old Vogt said he has not been contacted by the Mariners, who fired Dan Wilson last month following a disappointing 76-86 season.

Vogt spent one season as Seattle's bullpen coach in 2023 before being hired by Cleveland and that relationship helped fuel theories about a departure.

"I'll be in Cleveland," Vogt said three days after the Guardians were eliminated in the American League Championship Series by Tampa Bay. "I have not gotten a phone call."

While Vogt is adamant he's staying, it remains possible the Mariners could call the Guardians with a trade offer. Though rare, trades involving managers in Major League Baseball are not unprecedented, with the most recent one involving John Farrell going from Boston to Toronto in 2012.

Guardians president of baseball operations Chris Antonetti was asked about a potential pitch from the Mariners.

"I have every expectation that Voter is going to manage here for a really long time," Antonetti said, using Vogt's nickname. "We don't have any interest in Voter managing anywhere else."

Vogt signed a multiyear contract extension with Cleveland following the 2024 season. That deal was never made public and the club's secrecy about the contract's terms might have played a part in the rumors about a move.

A father of three, Vogt has been open about the difficulty of being away from his loved ones over an extended period. His wife, Alyssa, and their kids join him in the summer, but the months apart are hard on him.

"It's not just since I've been here. This has been my whole playing career," said Vogt, who played with six teams from 2012 to 2022. "It's very difficult living on the other side of the country, especially with my kids' age. My daughter's in high school, my boys are starting to get older, their activities are going up, so it's more challenging for them to get out here on a whim.

"But my wife's incredible and she reminds me every day that I'm where I'm supposed to be and I'm doing what I'm supposed to be doing. And she jokes, 'We don't need you anyway.' Not joking. It's the worst part of my job."

As for the job he did this season with Cleveland, Vogt deserves praise.

One of the league's youngest teams, the Guardians regrouped from a sluggish first half and, bolstered by several trade deadline acquisitions, caught Chicago and won the division. They then rallied from an 0-2 deficit to stun the White Sox in the AL Division Series.

Cleveland's magic disappeared against the Rays, extending baseball's current longest World Series drought to 78 years.

Through it all, Vogt believed the '26 Guardians would prevail.

"There was a belief that we were just going to do it," he said. "We were never out of it. It wasn't like '25 where we did this historical comeback, needed a bunch of help. We controlled our destiny and we went out and grabbed it and took it."

In other Guardians news, pitching coach Carl Willis, 65, will return for a 15th season with Cleveland (over two stints).

"He's given a ton to this organization and is insanely competitive," Antonetti said of Willis, who has helped develop five Cy Young winners during his career. "He really wants to win a World Series in Cleveland for Cleveland."

Also, Vogt said the curious lack of postseason use for starter Tanner Bibee was because the team wanted to lean on its left-handed pitchers. Vogt said he spoke with an "upset" Bibee before Game 6 of the ALCS.

"We ended up talking about a lot more than just baseball and had a similar conversation in his exit interview," Vogt said. "It was very candid. It was very open. He spoke his mind and we gave him our reasoning. Tanner's going to be a huge part of this team for a long time and I'm really excited about that."

stories.headline: In-the-dark Kane trying not to 'stress' over Monday's Ballon d'Or reveal
stories.summary: Bayern striker Harry Kane said he would prefer to know ahead of time whether he has won the Ballon D'Or, adding he is still in the dark over Monday's decision.
stories.body:
Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane said he would prefer to know ahead of time whether he has won the Ballon D'Or, adding he is still in the dark over Monday's decision.

The 33-year-old is the bookmakers' favourite to become the first Englishman to win the coveted prize since Michael Owen in 2001, but he faces competition from Barcelona's Lamine Yamal and Inter Miami CF's Lionel Messi among others on the 30-man shortlist.

As of 2024, organisers France Football insist they do not warn the winners in advance. That did not stop Real Madrid boycotting the event that year upon learning via a leak that Vinícius Júnior had been overlooked in favour of Rodri.

Kane scored for the tenth consecutive Champions League game on Wednesday as Bayern Munich drew 2-2 with Arsenal at Allianz Arena. Only Cristiano Ronaldo (11) has a longer streak in the competition's history and speaking to reporters after the game, Kane said: "They want everyone to go, all the big names there and there will be more people watching it if they don't know, so I can understand why.

"I think my wife would prefer to know and my family, it's very stressful for everyone. From my point of view, of course, I'd love to know to just kind of see and not have to wait throughout the whole night. But it is their decision, I can't control that. We'll have to just enjoy it and try not to stress out too much.

"I try not to think about it. Obviously it is hard not to. There are always rum ours flying around and you try to stay away from it. We have important games today and I know we have another important one on Sunday before the event on Monday so that's where my focus is.

"Of course I am going to try and enjoy Monday night as much as possible. It is a big occasion so we will have to wait and see."

Bayern have drawn two and won once in the League Phase of the UCL so far, leaving them in 14th place in the table. The Bundesliga champions face third-place Freiburg on Sunday as they try to remain atop of Germany's top flight.

stories.headline: UFC 333 preview and picks for featherweight, men's bantamweight titles
stories.summary: Check out the matchups and expert predictions for both championship fights at UFC 333 in Abu Dhabi.
stories.body:
How does a fighter know when to stop when they're fighting well?

It's a question that, unfortunately, rarely gets answered in MMA. For every athlete who retires from the sport on their own terms, there are at least two athletes being retired by the sport. It is rare for a fighter to go out on a win, and infinitely rare for a fighter to go out on top.

UFC featherweight champion Alexander Volkanovski (28-4) is starting to look that question in the face. Volkanovski will look to defend his title at UFC 333 on Saturday against 32-year-old Movsar Evloev (20-0) in Abu Dhabi, UAE. Volkanovski, 38, already is defying the rules of Father Time. In April 2025, he became the first fighter older than 35 to win a UFC championship belt in a weight class under 170 pounds. He defended that title in January against 31-year-old Diego Lopes.

In the past, Volkanovski has been dismissive, even comedic, of his age, starring in self-deprecating "Old Man Volk" skits on the internet. Ahead of UFC 333, however, he's been discussing age far more seriously, saying that any fight moving forward could be his last.

"There's a reason this is not often done," Volkanovski told ESPN. "I will bring up [my age], because I think it adds to the story. A lot of people are thinking about it. The young, undefeated guy -- facing the old, 38-year-old."

Evloev, of Russia, is one of the most proven title challengers in featherweight division history, with a perfect 10-0 record inside the Octagon, but he hasn't finished a single UFC opponent. He is a slight underdog against Volkanovski, according to DraftKings -- a credit to how good Volkanovski has looked, as well as lingering doubts on Evloev's ceiling.

Volkanovski, a two-time champion who suffered back-to-back knockout losses to Islam Makhachev and Ilia Topuria before regaining his title in 2025, told ESPN he believes he will actually look better than ever on Saturday, due to Evloev's style. The undefeated challenger is known primarily as a position-focused grappler, who might struggle to match Volkanovski's striking and scrambling ability.

"His style is a perfect matchup for me, I truly believe that," Volkanovski said. "I'm not delusional, saying I'm the best I've ever been at age 38. I'm not in my prime. But stylistically, I think you guys will be saying, 'I swear this is the best Volk we've ever seen.'"

Even if that is the case, odds say Volkanovski is tempting fate with every performance from this point forward. Male UFC fighters 38 and older have won 37% of their bouts all time, according to ESPN Research. Volkanovski has acknowledged as much and even proposed a "sendoff" title fight against 37-year-old lightweight champion Justin Gaethje next, after which they would both retire.

Volkanovski has stated he's taking it one fight at a time, but he is talking about retirement now, which shows he understands the decision is in front of him.

"One hundred percent, if I notice I'm slowing down or I'm taking more damage, [I'll retire]," Volkanovski said. "I said that before my last fight, too. A lot of people look at me saying that and say, 'Look how he's talking, his head isn't in it.' I'm just real and I'm honest. I said it before my last fight, and what happened? I went out there and made it look easy."

More storylines to watch

Dvalishvili looks to prove the last fight was an outlier
Merab Dvalishvili attempted to make history at the end of 2025, when he fought Petr Yan in his fourth men's bantamweight title defense of the calendar year. The feat has never been accomplished -- or even attempted -- and it proved to be too much as Dvalishvili lost a five-round decision. He later revealed he went into the bout with a significant knee injury and had a terrible camp. Dvalishvili (21-5) will try to recapture his title against Yan (20-5) in the UFC 333 co-main event.

Although he's admitted to tough circumstances around their last meeting, Dvalishvili has also said he doesn't regret pursuing UFC history and won't use those circumstances as an excuse, crediting Yan for the victory.

But the fighters' shared history has obviously raised the stakes for this Saturday. Dvalishvili and Yan have met twice, with Dvalishvili dominating their first meeting in March 2023. If Yan wins the trilogy, against a much fresher version of Dvalishvili than he saw in December, it could push Dvalishvili toward the back of the line for another title shot.

Not the last chance, but kind of the last chance
Not to put unnecessary pressure onto Aaron Pico's shoulders, but the truth is that any type of loss to Losene Keita -- a promising talent who is only 1-1 in the UFC -- would have heavy, long-lasting implications.

Pico, 30, has won 10 of his past 12 fights, but this is still a crossroads. He's been viewed as championship material since before his professional MMA debut, but has endured violent, memorable setbacks at various points in his career, including a spinning back elbow knockout loss to Lerone Murphy in his UFC debut 14 months ago. There is still massive potential in Pico, and he had an impressive bounce-back win against Patricio Pitbull in April, but he's in a risky position this weekend. He faces a dangerous but relatively unknown opponent in Keita after his original opponent, Arnold Allen, was forced off the card. Saturday's outcome will go a long way in determining how matchmakers and fans view him moving forward.

Coaches' questions and predictions for the title fights

Can Evloev significantly control Volkanovski on the ground?
Evloev is good everywhere, but Volkanovski has such an ability to game plan and show up in the big moments. Evloev is super big and strong. He has good standup, great transitions and ground control. But Volkanovski was able to get up after being taken down by Islam Makhachev. Are we just gonna forget that? Islam is now a welterweight. Volkanovski is so intelligent and so good at finding ways to exploit guys. His fight IQ is as good as anyone I've ever watched. He showed it against Lopes in their rematch in January. If Evloev cannot control Volk on the ground for long periods of time, Volkanovski will win a decision. And with the modern emphasis on damage when it comes to scoring, judges don't want to see you unsuccessfully try to hold someone down. Volkanovski by decision. -- Sayif Saud, Fortis MMA

Will age catch up to Volkanovski?
The biggest X factor is that unknown: At what point does Volkanovski's age slow him down? He's fighting one of the purest wrestlers/grapplers in the UFC in Evloev. I could see Evloev trying to prove he can stand with Volkanovski at times and win over the UFC, but I don't think that would be his smartest decision. Personally, I believe that "Old Man Volk" still has it. He's proven time and again he's going to win those key wrestling scrambles, and I believe he'll end up catching Movsar. It will be a grinder of a fight, but Volkanovski's experience being in there with bigger, stronger guys like Islam will pay off. Volkanovski by TKO. -- John Wood, Syndicate MMA

Can Dvavishvili hurt Yan with his hands?
We know that Yan has the physicality to compete with Merab's wrestling. He didn't avoid the takedown in their last fight -- he actually got more takedowns than Merab. That's a fact. And Yan on the feet is so dangerous, you have to give his standup the edge. If he comes in in great shape and can counter-wrestle and have the same physicality he did in December, he can win. The biggest technical question is whether Merab can create enough offense to get inside and hurt Yan with his hands. If the wrestling gets shut down, can he create offense? If Merab can hurt Yan on the feet, that changes the whole fight and throws it in favor of Merab. I've got Yan winning by a slight edge. -- Saud

Who will control the resets?
Yan needs to control the range, punish Merab's entries and continually invest in the body. He needs to establish the center and force Merab to initiate his wrestling from a distance, and intersect those entries with straight punches, body shots and uppercuts. I'd like to see him keep that lead arm frame, to establish his underhooks right away with his wrestling defense. He doesn't need to eliminate the takedown attempt, but he does need to make Merab pay for every failed attempt. Merab, meanwhile, has to weaponize pace, create chaos and disrupt Yan's comfort. He has to chain together multiple takedown attempts, so that even failed attempts affect Yan's rhythm. Who will control the resets? Merab thrives when one attack becomes three or four; Yan thrives when he's able to reset and return to technical striking. I lean Yan by decision again. --Eric Nicksick, Xtreme Couture

stories.headline: St. Louis GK Bürki stretchered off after collision in Open Cup final
stories.summary: St. Louis goalkeeper Roman Bürki was taken to the hospital after taking a knock to the head during the U.S. Open Cup final against the Columbus Crew.
stories.body:
St. Louis City goalkeeper Roman Bürki was taken to the hospital after taking a knock to the head in a collision during his team's U.S. Open Cup final win over the Columbus Crew on Wednesday night.

In an attempt to make a save in the 70th minute, Bürki took a knee to the head from Crew winger Anass Zaroury. He remained on the ground to receive medical attention before being stretchered off the field.

Bürki was able to wave to supporters as he was taken away from the pitch. St. Louis confirmed to ESPN that Bürki was conscious and moving all extremities on his way to the hospital.

"He is currently alert and in good spirits. The club's medical staff will continue to monitor his condition and the team will provide additional updates as they become available," the club later said in a statement on X.

The score was tied 0-0 at the time of the injury, but St. Louis went on to win the game in a shootout after Burki's backup Ben Lundt made a save to help his team beat the Crew 5-3 on spot kicks.

The win earned St. Louis, which began play in MLS in 2023, its first trophy in club history.

St. Louis City captain Bürki had 43 touches and three crucial saves before the injury. He played an integral role in maintaining the 0-0 draw before being replaced by Lundt after the head injury.

Bürki, who joined St. Louis from Borussia Dortmund in 2022, stopped a corner kick from Brais Méndez that appeared to be goalbound and a flurry of other shots just before sustaining his injury.

Eleven minutes of injury time was added due to Bürki's injury, but neither team scored before the end of regulation despite Columbus outshooting St. Louis 16-3, so the game went to extra time and penalties.

stories.headline: 'No regrets': why Kangaroos prop made switch from Tonga
stories.summary: Keaon Koloamatangi has revealed why he couldn't knock back the opportunity to represent Australia at the World Cup after previously doing the same with Tonga.
stories.body:
Keaon Koloamatangi has revealed why he couldn't knock back the opportunity to represent Australia at the World Cup after previously doing the same with Tonga.

In recent years, the international scene has mostly showcased players with multiple heritages moving across from tier-one sides such as New Zealand and Australia to play for nations such as Samoa and Tonga in particular.

Koloamatangi went the other way, switching from Tonga to Australia before last year's Ashes tour after previously representing the Mate Ma'a on 10 occasions, including the 2022 World Cup.

"I just want to experience everything. I was lucky enough to play for Tonga in the last World Cup in England," Koloamatangi said

"I think if Australia comes calling, it's not something you can turn your back on. It's probably the best team you can make, and it's something I want to look back on, knowing I always dreamt of doing it as a kid."

Koloamatangi, who will join St George Illawarra next season from South Sydney, has a deep appreciation for both nations and does not regard his choice this time as valuing one side of his heritage over the other.

The 28-year-old will play prop against Fiji at Suncorp Stadium on Sunday night as a proud Kangaroo.

"I played for Tonga, I've play Origin, and I wanted to play for all the nations that I am eligible for," he said.

"It's something I'm really proud of because I'm just as Australian as I am Tongan. I was born Australian and my dad's Tongan. For me, I just wanted to experience a World Cup in the Australian colours, and I've got a lot of great mates here too."

Koloamatangi admits it was "a tough decision" but the classy response of Tonga coach Kristian Woolf reassured him.

"I spoke to Woolfy and he was very grateful for the conversation I had with him. He was respectful and accepted my decision. I have no regrets," Koloamatangi said.

"I loved my time with Tonga, with the atmosphere they get and the crowds they get.

"They're such a small country, and seeing them on the big stage now I've been being blessed to be a part of it."

There is a chance Tonga and Australia could meet in the World Cup semi-final or final.

Tonga's 30-12 win over England in the opening round has them on track to reach the final-four.

"I watched the game last week and was so proud of how they turned up for their nation," Koloamatangi said.

"Obviously, I want Australia to win, but if we weren't to win, I'll be cheering the Tongans all the way. I wish nothing but the best for them."

stories.headline: Max Verstappen warns 'out of control' bumps at U.S. Grand Prix pose risks for drivers' spines
stories.summary: Max Verstappen has said Formula 1 drivers risk long-term damage from venues with "out of control" bumps like Austin's Circuit of the Americas (COTA), citing a concerning recent X-ray he's seen of his own back.
stories.body:
Max Verstappen has said Formula 1 drivers risk long-term damage from venues with "out of control" bumps like Austin's Circuit of the Americas (COTA), citing a concerning recent X-ray he's seen of his own back.

After winning the last race in Singapore, Verstappen quipped that he will "probably need a new spine" ahead of the next race, Sunday's U.S. Grand Prix.

The four-time world champion went back to that topic on Thursday during a media session previewing the race, stressing that it was no laughing matter.

"It was extremely badly bumpy," Verstappen said on watching a World Endurance Championship (WEC) race at the circuit earlier this year. "So I'm not really looking forward to that, to be honest, for your spine.

"You know, I was joking about that, of course, in the last race. But it's not really a joke to be honest. Because we mentioned this already for years that it's actually getting a bit out of control. And I'm sure that tomorrow is going to be quite tough to find the right compromises around this track [with set-up]."

Verstappen elaborated just how extreme the bumps can be at high speed.

He added: "So last year, for example, you pull around 5, 6G [-force] in a corner, but I had some impacts, like vertical load, which was like over 9G on my spine, which I can tell you is really not fun. And especially the older you get, you think about that more and more.

"That's not what you want. And with these cars, especially under braking, you bottom out way harder because when the wings close and the right hand comes down, under braking, it's actually a very stressful moment. And I know around here, in some places, it's very bumpy under braking.

"And especially when it's like these kind of awkward bumps, not just bumps from the track getting colder, but just going, I don't know, the surface underneath the soil just moving up and down. Sometimes very hard to expect, or if you're like a tiny bit offline, you don't know what is there because no one really drives there sometimes. So, yeah, it's really not nice.

"And I think sometimes people don't really understand that. Because, yeah, I can tell you from the checks that I've done from my spine, the bottom end doesn't look that great, the spine. So I know that's part of racing. I know that can be part of sport, but it's, of course, also further damage from the cars that we had the last few years. And now if we continue with driving, or finding this acceptable to drive on, then, yeah, you are going to suffer with that much more. And people can say, yeah, but there are worse sports out there for damage to parts of your body, for sure."

- Carlos Sainz on F1 season concluding in Middle East: 'Very difficult to be convinced right now'

- Kimi Antonelli is on the brink of F1 history -- but first, there's a car to wash and pranks to pull

- Oliver Bearman 'ready to fight for podiums' with eye on joining top-four team

Other drivers echoed Verstappen's opinions on the bumpy track.

When Verstappen's comments were put to reigning world champion Lando Norris, he said circuits should be held to higher standards when it comes to track smoothness.

Norris revealed it is so extreme at some places he's been forced to take headache tablets to counteract the pain.

"I would say yes," he said on whether he agreed with Verstappen. "If you build a new track now, the rules, the regulation of building a new track, the tolerances you have to be within are pretty small. [COTA] certainly doesn't fit anywhere close to what those regulations are now, I'm going to say, but it's an old track, not a new track.

"I mean, it's pretty bad, like, there's a lot of places I need to take headache tablets before I go out, simply because it's so bumpy and, and you're hitting your head pretty hard against the headrests and things because of the bumps. So it's certainly not a nice thing. But there's not much we can do.

"I mean, we complain about it, it's stuff we brought up many, many times, but there's only so much we can complain about things.

"But he's certainly right."

stories.headline: How a UConn influence is helping fuel the Valkyries in WNBA Finals
stories.summary: Former Huskies Gabby Williams, Tiffany Hayes, Kiah Stokes and Kaitlyn Chen look to help Golden State even the Finals.
stories.body:
With her teammates huddled around her, Gabby Williams leaned in, seemingly looking at every one of them as she gestured and pointed emphatically. Williams' Golden State Valkyries had just lost for the second straight game, falling behind the Atlanta Dream 2-1 in the WNBA Finals.

Williams sent a message to her teammates. Now it's time for the Valkyries to try to send one to the Dream as they attempt to rally in the best-of-seven series, which continues Saturday (1 p.m. ET) in Game 4 at State Farm Arena in Atlanta.

If they can, the Valkyries will be channeling a large amount of UConn Huskies influence.

Williams is one of four Valkyries -- along with Tiffany Hayes, Kiah Stokes and Kaitlyn Chen -- who won national championships at UConn. Their paths to get here and the roles they have played varied, but they all were influenced by the women's college program that has won the most NCAA titles (12) and sent the most players (54) to the WNBA.

"Every kid that spent that time here has certain qualities that make you win championships," UConn coach Geno Auriemma told reporters in Connecticut earlier this month. "And I don't think I'd be overstating it that if those four were not on that team, they wouldn't be where they are today."

The Golden State franchise and UConn don't have much in common in terms of history. The expansion Valkyries launched last year. Auriemma is entering his 42nd season at UConn. But under coach Natalie Nakase, the Valkyries already have developed an elite defensive commitment that Auriemma's teams always have. Golden State's style worked in beating the Dallas Wings 2-1 in the first round and sweeping the Las Vegas Aces 3-0 in the semifinals.

It also helped them prevail 68-64 in Game 1 of the Finals this past Saturday in San Francisco. But in Games 2 and 3, the Dream have cracked the code, flipping the Valkyries' combined 36 turnovers into 46 points to win 79-65 on Monday in San Francisco and 97-71 on Wednesday in Atlanta.

To even the series, the Valkyries need to make Game 4 on Saturday look more like Game 1. Cutting down on turnovers is the first job, but getting back their swag is important, too. The No. 2 Valkyries are the higher seed, and they knocked off the defending-champion Aces. But Golden State hasn't looked like that team since halftime of Game 2.

Williams' animated postgame callout to her teammates could help reignite the fire.

"I think passion and emotion in sports is huge," Nakase said. "What's really good about our team is we embrace it. We love the fight. We love the screaming."

Even if they don't all show it the same way.

"This is the Finals, is it not emotional?" Stokes said, then added with her trademark deadpan humor, "Not everyone is emotionless like me."

Hayes -- who is more on the passionate side in her playing style and personality -- is the oldest of the "West Coast Huskies." The 37-year-old guard won NCAA titles in 2009 and 2010 with UConn, then in 2012 was drafted by Atlanta. She spent her first 10 seasons with the Dream, then was traded to the Connecticut Sun in 2023.

At the end of that year, she announced her retirement, which didn't last long. She played for Las Vegas in 2024, then joined former Aces assistant Nakase in Golden State the past two seasons.

Hayes is seeking her first WNBA title. To get it, the Valkyries must beat the franchise with which Hayes spent most of her pro career. Her UConn days might be pretty far in the rearview mirror, but she still has Huskies DNA.

"It starts with the type of players they recruit there," Hayes said. "Being able to take constructive criticism and stay a positive person. I was that person when they recruited me, and it's really carried with me from my time there.

"Coach always wanted me to get better, and though that came with some hard times, that's part of growing. I really respect when people are that way with me, because it has really helped me as a player."

Stokes has won three WNBA titles, all with the Aces. She opted to move to Golden State as a free agent this season, as did Williams, who previously was with the Seattle Storm. They were teammates for one season at UConn, 2014-15. Stokes was a senior and Williams a freshman as the Huskies went 38-1, winning the national championship.

Stokes has a more low-key, laid-back personality, but the fire can come out in her on court, especially with her specialty: defense. Stokes averaged 5.8 rebounds and 1.7 blocks in the regular season, numbers that have jumped to 9.6 and 2.6 in the playoffs.

"One thing UConn taught me was to play through adversity when things aren't going your way," Stokes said about an attitude that can help Golden State in this series. "Geno would always make the practices so hard, the games would seem easier."

Williams has led the Valkyries in scoring this season (14.4 PPG in the regular season and 21.2 in the playoffs). But she praises Stokes for doing all the detail-oriented things that don't always get much acclaim yet are crucial to success, such as screening and passing.

She also cites Stokes' mentality, which Williams shares and thinks is the hallmark of UConn's program.

"The biggest thing with UConn culture is putting the team first," Williams said. "Giving up a good shot for a great shot. Putting winning and culture before individual accolades."

As for Chen, she doesn't seem to mind being underestimated. To the contrary, she not only expects it, she has turned it into her superpower.

"She doesn't care if other people don't believe in her," Nakase said. "Kaitlyn wants to be the best."

Chen spent three seasons at Princeton playing for former UConn player Carla Berube, then transferred her senior year to UConn. Chen won the 2025 NCAA title alongside fellow guards Paige Bueckers and Azzi Fudd, the past two WNBA No. 1 draft picks.

Chen was selected No. 30 in 2025 by the Valkyries, bringing the California native back to her home state. Third-round picks often don't make WNBA rosters, but Chen is in her second season. She has appeared in every game in 2026, averaging 7.2 points in the regular season and 5.7 in the playoffs.

Even though Chen was at UConn just one season, with the influence of Berube's coaching, it almost felt like she was a Huskies-type player all along.

"At UConn, you're playing in such a specific system that really values defense and values ball control on offense," Chen said. "I feel like it's similar to how we do things here.

"Playing in that system, for Coach Auriemma, and also getting to play alongside so many really great players, helped me figure out how to play within my role."

There have been so many UConn players in the WNBA, Auriemma almost always has multiple rooting interests during the playoffs. Another of his former players, Renee Montgomery, is an Atlanta Dream co-owner and executive. But on court, the Valkyries' four former Huskies are carrying the UConn torch to the end of the WNBA season.

"I'm really proud of all of them," Auriemma said, "and that's probably the one team that I've watched play the most."

Stokes said she doesn't necessarily think that often about the UConn connection, since there are great WNBA players from all over. But at times she is reminded there is something tangible to it. Stokes recalled first talking to Nakase about it when both were with the Aces.

"She loves UConn players because they have the mindset, the work ethic," Stokes said. "They understand the game."

Alexa Philippou contributed to this report.

stories.headline: Way-too-early AFL tiers: There's a clear flag favourite; 'silly season' winners and losers
stories.summary: Who are the 2027 flag favourites? Who are the legitimate contenders? And who should already be booking September holidays? It's our way-too-early edition of AFL tiers.
stories.body:
The 2026 AFL season is done and dusted, but that hasn't stopped ESPN's senior writer Jake Michaels from turning his attention to next year. Who are the 2027 flag favourites? Who are the legitimate contenders? And who should already be booking September holidays? It's our way-too-early edition of AFL tiers!

All of our best footy content, now on Instagram. Follow @espnfooty here!

Your new premiership favourite

1. HAWTHORN

Who knows if the Hawks would have been premiers this year if not for Hugh McCluggage's heroics late in that dramatic preliminary final at the MCG. There's certainly a real argument they would have gone all the way. This side, which is expertly coached by Sam Mitchell, just added Zach Merrett and Ben King to its best 23, two more experienced players desperate for flag success. There won't be many games the Hawks don't start favourite in next year. Even if this club's 2027 season over/under was set at preliminary final weekend, I'd still be taking the over.

Should be great, but there are some questions

2. BRISBANE

3. FREMANTLE

4. SYDNEY

The Lions just completed a remarkable three-peat and it certainly wouldn't have been outrageous for them to hold top spot here. But losing Lachie Neale and Chris Fagan -- arguably the two most important pieces of the club's modern-day dynasty -- cannot be underestimated. How do they fill those seismic gaps? The Dockers were the dominant team of the home and away season and if we played out the last four minutes of the Grand Final 100 times they probably win 99 of them. Instead, Fremantle has to spend all offseason dwelling on the greatest missed opportunity in club history. How do they respond in 2027? As for the Swans, who are always somewhere around the mark, nobody can really be sure what to expect after the Pullman Hotel saga. So many fascinating questions.

Silly season winners

5. GEELONG

6. WESTERN BULLDOGS

7. CARLTON

8. COLLINGWOOD

Each of these teams will be counting down the days until the 2027 season after drastically improving their lists during the trade and free agency window. The Cats landed the dynamic Toby Greene, significantly upgraded their ruck department with the singing of Rowan Marshall, and bolstered their defensive stocks with Jordan Ridley. The Bulldogs scored the biggest prize of all in Zak Butters, but they were also able to pry away Jordon Butts from the Crows, a much needed acquisition to what's been a shaky defence. The Blues will go into next season with Joel Amartey, Lachie Whitfield, and almost certainly father-son talent Cody Walker, while the Magpies added dual Brownlow medallist Lachie Neale and 2024 Coleman Medal winner Jesse Hogan.

Silly season losers

9. MELBOURNE

10. ADELAIDE

While a bunch of teams we'd expect to be in the fifth-to-10th range clearly improved their best 23, the Demons and Crows did nothing of the sort. Adelaide literally brought in nobody and will have to deal with the loss of key defender Jordon Butts, who departed as a free agent for the Bulldogs. Melbourne did sign several names, but do we think any of Zane Duursma, Will McLachlan, and Bodie Ryan can be needle movers in 2027? But hey, these were two sides I was down on this year and both ultimately outperformed expectations. Perhaps they do have it all figured out...

It's now or never

11. GOLD COAST

12. NORTH MELBOURNE

13. ST KILDA

If not now, then when? The Suns rocketed to co-flag favouritism this time last year after signing Christian Petracca and Jamarra Ugle-Hagan. They ultimately won just nine games and finished 13th on the ladder. Disastrous. Damien Hardwick is under serious pressure to get more out of this list. Meanwhile, the Kangaroos haven't played finals in a decade, but there's some newfound optimism after the senior coaching appointment of highly regarded Jaymie Graham and the signing of Nick Blakey, the biggest name the club has attracted in a decade. The Saints also need to show something early in 2027 or Ross Lyon could be on his way out ... again! But the real worry is not doing enough to ensure star midfielder Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera signs on.

It's going to be another long year

14. PORT ADELAIDE

15. GWS

16. WEST COAST

17. RICHMOND

18. ESSENDON

Perhaps I'm being a tad harsh on Port, who were pretty competitive this year. But at the end of the day we're taking Zak Butters out of a side that won just seven games. The Giants lost four of their best players in Toby Greene, Jesse Hogan, Lachie Whitfield, and Kieren Briggs, and will be relying heavily on their younger talent next year. And then there's the Eagles, Tigers, and Bombers -- three teams that combined for just nine wins this year. We all expect these sides to be somewhere around the bottom of the ladder.

By the time they were going for their third straight Champions League title in 2017-18, Real Madrid had mastered the art of easing in. In 2016-17, they finished behind Borussia Dortmund in their group and constantly needed their trademarked, late-game Real Madrid magic to secure points before igniting in the knockout rounds. For the three-peat, they finished second in their group behind Tottenham Hotspur, but mostly rolled in the spring again.

Paris Saint-Germain have certainly learned that you don't have to look your sharpest early on. Two seasons ago, in their first of what is currently a two-year title streak -- and in the first year for the expanded league phase structure -- they narrowly beat Girona in their first match and then lost three of their next four matches before finally starting to click into place in December. They won their next five Champions League matches by a combined 18 goals, knocked off top-seeded Liverpool in penalties in the round of 16 and ... mostly rolled from there.

You can play with fire without getting burned, but Luis Enrique has decided he really doesn't want to. PSG started far better last year, winning four of their first five league phase matches, and this fall they've been all business: After a 6-1 tuneup against Slovan Bratislava to start, they've beaten Manchester City and Barcelona, each by multiple goals. They were winless in their first four matches in all competitions in this campaign, but when the Champions League began, so did their season.

- UCL Power Rankings: Can anyone slow PSG down?

- Talking Points: Man United's mess, PSG lose Kvara, more

- Dawson: Who are Como, the destination club making waves

Along with a 2-2 draw between Arsenal and Bayern Munich, PSG's 4-2 win over Barcelona was the most noteworthy result of Champions League Matchday 3, even if Khvicha Kvaratskhelia's ACL tear cast a bit of a pall on the proceedings. But five teams continued their perfect starts -- PSG, Real Madrid, Liverpool, Aston Villa and Real Betis -- and all of the most likely candidates to win next week's Ballon d'Or made exciting plays.

The league phase keeps rolling, but here are soccer's five main characters as we move past Matchday 3.

Main character No. 1: Harry Kane's closing argument

The voting for this year's Ballon d'Or, which will be awarded this coming Monday, closed a while ago. While the prediction market odds were shifting toward Barca's Lamine Yamal for a while, they appear to have homed in on Bayern Munich's Harry Kane as the likely winner, and justifiably so. He simply had the best year of anyone, winning three trophies, leading England to the World Cup semifinals for a second time and -- oh yeah -- scoring 73 goals with eight assists in 65 total matches. Yamal had only 25 and 20, respectively, in the same period. England teammate (and Wednesday adversary) Declan Rice declared him incredibly deserving, and just in case there was any lingering doubt, Kane put his skill set on display once again in Bayern's 2-2 draw with Arsenal.

The match itself was impacted by absences. Bayern's Michael Olise (red card suspension), Joshua Kimmich (family bereavement) and Jamal Musiala (injury) missed the match, and Arsenal's Bukayo Saka left with injury 10 minutes in. Bayern's Luis Díaz also left with what he later called a minor injury late in the match, and manager Vincent Kompany was even a question mark for the match due to both illness and a hip issue.

These are two of the deepest teams in the world, however, and both lineups still featured plenty of star power. Alphonso Davies ostensibly played on the left wing instead of at left back for most of the evening, and he made the most of the opportunity, getting on the end of a long pass and sending an equalizing goal past David Raya in the 35th minute.

The sender of that beautiful long pass? Kane.

Who both set up and converted the penalty that put Bayern ahead (until Rice's late equalizer)? Kane. That was one of four shots he put on goal, and while Bayern only managed to break Arsenal's defensive line twice with completed passes, Kane was the passer on both. Bayern aren't used to getting anything less than three points at home, but in this case, playing with a short-handed squad against a team that thumped them 3-1 in last year's league phase, a draw was a pretty solid result.

Bayern will visit third-place Freiburg in Bundesliga action on Sunday, and then we'll find out if Kane's Ballon d'Or time has arrived. He would be Bayern's first winner since Karl-Heinz Rummenigge in 1981 (justice for Robert Lewandowski) and the first English winner since Michael Owen in 2001.

Kane isn't a stranger to awards. Name another person who has won the Premier League Golden Boot, the World Cup Golden Boot, Bundesliga Player of the Season and the Millwall Young Player of the Year award and has also been named a member of the Order of the British Empire -- you can't. But between the overbearing presence of Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo over individual awards, and the fact that he has only recently played for a team that regularly wins hardware, Kane has yet to finish in the top three of the Ballon d'Or voting. And now he'd be a deserving winner at 33.

It's a pretty remarkable tale for a player who has spent 15 years honing weaknesses into strengths and becoming a better and better player.

Main character No. 2: Vitinha's perfect role

At a broad level, nothing really went right for Paris Saint-Germain against Barcelona on Tuesday. Three starters had to be subbed off injured in the first hour, and superstar Khvicha Kvaratskhelia tore his ACL. Ferran Torres, thrust into action when Ousmane Dembélé came out after 20 minutes, created three great opportunities, but hit the post once and had two efforts saved. Désiré Doué scored to give the Parisiens a first-half lead, but Xavi Espart equalized early in the second half, and Lamine Yamal, looking as dangerous as ever, equalized for Barca again after PSG got an unlikely goal from Lucas Hernández (his first in over two years).

As ever, however, PSG had Vitinha.

If you told me the Line-Breaking Passes statistic was invented specifically to measure Vitinha's greatness, I'd believe you: He had 15 of them against Barca, and 12 were completed while under pressure from Barca's relentless midfield. He actually led PSG in both passes that broke the attacking line (eight) and passes that broke the midfield line (six), and he trailed only Doue in total carry distance (250 meters) as well. And in the 81st minute, with the buzz from Yamal's goal having not completely worn off yet, Vitinha went into "I'll do it myself" mode.

Vitinha remains the hinge for PSG's absurd successes; considering the injuries and constant shuffling up front, you could make an easy case that he's their most important player. And that just makes me madder at Roberto Martinez.

I covered a majority of Portugal's matches at the 2026 FIFA World Cup, and I was pretty excited about it considering how much I've come to enjoy Vitinha's PSG play; he's a brilliant ball progressor with a take-charge streak, somehow making him a combination of Pedri and Steven Gerrard. But he was mostly ineffective in the World Cup. While he averaged about the same number of touches as he does for PSG, Portugal's refusal/inability to progress the ball with purpose meant that he was mostly working the ball horizontally.

Some players are simply better for club than country, or vice versa, so Vitinha's struggles don't have to mean anything specific. But man, is it hard to believe that; Portugal featured three of Vitinha's PSG teammates (João Neves, Nuno Mendes and Gonçalo Ramos), plus three members of a Manchester City team that loved possession and occasionally sexy ball progression as much as PSG (Rúben Dias, Matheus Nunes, Bernardo Silva). But none of the team's infinite number of creatives seemed to match their club levels and while it makes me a bit of a broken record, it's hard to ignore the other main subplot for Portugal's World Cup disappointment: Martinez's insistence on playing Cristiano Ronaldo up front.

Portugal's attack got consistently gummed up as Ronaldo walked around, slowed the attack down whenever he was on the ball and contributed nothing to pressing structures. Almost insultingly, Vitinha was subbed out of every match and averaged only 76.2 minutes per appearance; Ronaldo finished four of five matches and averaged 88.2 minutes.

Even in the recent international break, with Martinez out and Ronaldo playing a minimal role before his petulant walk-out, Vitinha's role was relatively un-PSG-like. He contributed more in attack, with far more shots and expected assists, more ball recoveries and more line-breaking passes received but far fewer overall touches.

Ronaldo alone wasn't impacting his role, but Portugal was certainly more effective without him. Thank goodness the Ronaldo era is finally over ... right? RIGHT??

Well, whatever. At least we get to see Vitinha in full glory in the Champions League.

Main character No. 3: Virgil van Dijk and Liverpool's ongoing rebuild

Maybe Sir Alex Ferguson's most impressive trait was his ability to regenerate a roster. His vaunted Class of 1992 certainly drove a lot of United's success in the late-1990s and 2000s, but United finished in the top three of England's first division for 21 consecutive seasons and only once went more than one year without a title. (That was at the start of the Roman Abramovich era at Chelsea, when the Blues barged into what had been a two-team title picture with United and Arsenal. United responded to a three-year drought with three consecutive titles.)

As even Pep Guardiola learned, keeping a title-level roster going, without loyalty and age eventually producing a tired lineup -- and without burning out -- is ridiculously hard. For all of Manchester City's spending advantages (legal and otherwise), Guardiola resigned last spring after pulling only a 43% Fergie (nine straight top-threes). After six titles in seven years, staleness overtook City in 2024-25, and they needed a huge burst of January spending to pull off a distant third place in the Premier League race. They improved only marginally last season, though they've started this season beautifully, despite epic noise, under Enzo Maresca.

West of Manchester, Liverpool is pulling off an even more awkward transition. They're on their third manager in four seasons, and of the 16 players who started at least eight matches during their semi-surprising 2024-25 Premier League title run, nine are gone, and three more are at least 30 years old. Dominik Szoboszlai, Ryan Gravenberch, Alexis Mac Allister and Cody Gakpo give them a solid base of players who are both in their prime and have been around a while, but age in both attack and defense forced Liverpool to regenerate, and two summers in, we're still seeing almost frantically up-and-down results.

Their scoring has improved by 23% this season in all competitions, from 1.77 goals per game to 2.18. Two of last season's disappointing signings -- Alexander Isak and Florian Wirtz -- have started to contribute at a more consistent level, with six goals and four assists between them. For all the scrutiny piled onto him, Wirtz leads his team in ground duels won (37), chances created (28), shot attempts (25), line-breaking passes received (157), line-breaking passes in the attacking third (26) and ball recoveries (48), and he now has a goal and two assists in his past three matches. Beyond Wirtz and Isak, however, Andoni Iraola's frequently aggressive tactics have produced opportunities for just about everyone in a red shirt: Ten players have scored at least one goal, and 11 have at least one assist.

Liverpool are playing fun ball again and have scored 12 goals in three matches since a disappointing 3-0 loss to Manchester City. They've also allowed three goals in three of their past four matches. Five of their 11 matches this season have featured at least four combined goals. This is great for neutrals, but it's also a sign that defensive fragility is their next issue to address.

That brings us to the Virgil van Dijk conundrum. The Liverpool legend remains a vital cog in buildup play and ball progression -- he's first on the team in touches, passes completed, passes received, progressive carries, progressive passes, line-breaking passes, aerial duels, you name it. He's also 35 and a bit more error-prone, and Iraola's high risk profile means he's getting exposed a bit more in transition.

Tuesday's match against Villarreal began with one of the biggest errors of Van Dijk's Liverpool tenure.

Sergi Cardona scored a beautiful transition goal to put Villarreal up 2-0 before the 30th minute, too, but Liverpool's attacking prowess eventually won out. Mac Allister scored a pair of goals, teenager Rio Ngumoha assisted goals for Ronald Araújo and Mac Allister in probably the best match of his career, and Wirtz put away an eventual 4-3 win in transition.

This was all of Liverpool's upside and downside in the extreme, and it made them more difficult than ever to evaluate. Their moments of brilliance gave them three points after devastating errors dug them a hole. Van Dijk was poor -- "obviously I tried, but it was a bad day at the office personally," he told the media afterward -- but it didn't end up mattering. I'm not sure how much longer this period of Liverpool transition lasts, and I'm not sure how much longer Van Dijk's excellent traits outweigh age, but hey, at least the Reds are entertaining as hell.

Main character No. 4: Sasa and the first-timers

We once again saw plenty of goals in this week's Champions League action -- a delightful 74 in 18 matches, over two per team. Manchester City casually knocked in five without Erling Haaland against AEK Athens, while seven scored four, including Galatasaray in a campaign-saving comeback against Lille, Como in the latest humiliation of Manchester United and Liverpool and Napoli in matching 4-3 wins over Villarreal and Bodø/Glimt, respectively. Hell, five more scored three goals. Aston Villa moved to nine points and 12 goals with a 3-1 win over Viking, and the ever-watchable Club Brugge chugged right along, 3-0, over Lens. Hell, Bayern even coaxed a match with four total goals out of Arsenal.

We're going to focus on someone else, though. While most of these matches will be forgotten six months from now -- hey, I enjoy the league phase perfectly fine, but there's definitely an "endless content with minimal jeopardy" aspect to it -- LASK's win over Sporting CP will end up part of club lore.

LASK won their first Austrian Bundesliga crown in 61 years last spring, and while they've spent plenty of time in the Europa League and Conference League of late, a win over Celtic in August (they came back from 3-0 down after the first leg) qualified them for the Champions League for the first time in, well, 61 years, back when it was the European Cup. They've beaten Inter Milan, Sporting CP, Werder Bremen and other bigger names in previous tournaments, but on Wednesday they scored their first official Champions League win. And a familiar name played a major role.

You may have last seen Sasa Kalajdzic during one of the wildest sequences of the World Cup. After Algeria scored a shocking 100-pass goal to take a late 3-2 lead on Austria in the final matchday, in a match in which both teams would advance with a draw, the stoic Kalajdzic used his 6-foot-7 frame to head in an equalizer moments later. It was his first goal for Austria since overtime in the Euro 2020 round of 16. The guy knows his moments. And in the 63rd minute in Lisbon on Wednesday, he put LASK ahead 2-1. They would lead the rest of the way.

Kalajdzic has suffered three ACL tears in recent years, and he has enjoyed only one season with double-digit goals since he scored 10 for Admira Wacker Amateure in Austria's Regionalliga East 10 years ago. But no one can accuse him of failing to make memories.

Main character No. 5: El Clasico

In the late 2000s, the Premier League's money cannon began to reap dividends. Between 2005-09, English teams took 12 of the 20 spots in Champions League semifinals, six of 10 in the finals and won the title in 2005 (Liverpool over AC Milan) and 2008 (Manchester United over countrymate Chelsea). Sustained brilliance from Manchester United and Arsenal, plus a Roman Abramovich-backed charge from Chelsea, gave England a seemingly permanent place atop the soccer hierarchy.

That dominance came to a (temporary) halt, however, at the hands of two Spanish giants. Between 2009-18, either Barcelona or Real Madrid won seven of 10 Champions League titles, and English teams made only four finals appearances with one win (Chelsea over Bayern in 2012). Barcelona's playing style became the model for nearly every monied team in the world, give or take, and Real Madrid overwhelmed opponents with talent and late-game magic.

In 2026, the Premier League has grown as dominant as ever. Five different English teams have made the Champions League finals since 2019 (three have won), and English teams have won the past two Europa Leagues (it was an all-English final in 2025) and three of the past four Conference Leagues.

Granted, PSG's own financial dominance has conquered the Champions League the past two years -- and handed Barcelona their first loss of the season on Tuesday -- but Spain's dynamic duo might be ready to disrupt England's gravitational pull a bit more. Especially if Yan Diomande is ready to do a little bit more of this.

I'm not sure it's possible to strike a ball any sweeter than that.

Real Madrid were at their most attractive in the second half, getting goals from Arda Güler, Kylian Mbappé and Diomande on their way to a 4-1 romp over RB Leipzig. They've scored four goals in six of their 12 matches this season -- 33 in all -- and Vinícius Júnior hasn't even gotten going yet. They got xG'd to hell in a 1-0 loss to Real Betis in September (20 shots, 3.5 xG, zero goals), and they got Atletico'd in a 2-1 Madrid derby loss, but they've won 10 matches, and a win over Barcelona in the first El Clasico of the season on Sunday would pull them to within three points of the top of LaLiga. For all of the great headlines Barca have earned to start the season, Real Madrid aren't far behind.

Barca have earned those headlines, by the way. Lamine Yamal just played on a losing team for the first time since April 8, and he still managed to do this.

Raphinha missed a month of action after playing the best ball of his life, and Barcelona kept scoring loads of goals without him. Yamal already has 10 goals and 10 assists in all competitions, and Raphinha has 14 and three, respectively. Anthony Gordon, with his three lungs, was born to play for Hansi Flick, while Fermín López, Karim Adeyemi and Gabriel Jesus have combined for 13 goals. And Barca's midfield depth is so ridiculous that Flick was able to bring Gavi and Rodri off the bench on Tuesday. They fell to PSG, and Flick's high-wire style will always leave them a bit vulnerable in the back. But they play the most seductive and watchable ball in the world, and I think they're allowed one loss every six months.

In other words, Sunday's El Clasico (Sunday, 4 p.m. ET, ABC) could be something else.
